newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage rescue ends uncertainty for investors.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage rescue ends uncertainty for investors.

text.p: The military assault that ended Peru's 126-day hostage crisis on Tuesday also put an end to investor uncertainty and should allow the economy to surge forward on its path of sustained growth, analysts said.
"The element of uncertainty that hung around investors has been eliminated," Miguel Palomino, an analyst at investment bank Merrill Lynch in Peru, told Reuters.
Latin America's longest hostage siege ended when President Alberto Fujimori ordered 140 armed forces' commandos to storm the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.

Despite predictions of a heavier death toll in the event of a military solution, only one hostage died in the operation. Two soldiers and all 14 of the jungle-trained Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels also died.

Haldor Lopez Alba of the University of Lima's Economic Investigative Center predicted a positive reaction to the rescue operation, which would benefit not only Peru but would help foreign capital in-flows into Latin America as a whole.
"Many investors were unsure about coming to Peru. A positive effect can be expected in the short term for the country and in the long term for the region in general," Lopez said.

While the Marxist rebels' spectacular takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence on Dec. 17 initially wounded foreigners' confidence, as the dust settled these investors increasingly saw the crisis as an isolated event.

But with 72 VIP captives under rebel arms, Peru was always in danger of having its risk-weightings reassessed if the security forces botched a rescue attempt or if the MRTA was perceived to have won too much from a possible negotiated end.
"This is going to improve the perception of Peru from abroad. The perception of country-risk is very important when investors take decisions," Palomino said.

Peruvian Brady bonds reacted positively to the results of the assault. At 6:30 p.m. EDT (2330 GMT) Tuesday, Peru PDI bonds were 7/8 higher at 58-1/4 and the country's FLIRBs were 1-3/4 better at 53-1/4 bid.
Jose Marquez, analyst at Peruvian brokerage Abila y Calpe, called the military operation a "success" that would result in a surge on the Lima stock exchange.
"It will give Fujimori a boost and immediately stimulate the bolsa," Marquez said.

Japanese companies quickly reacted to the end of the crisis, saying they were relieved at the release of employees held for four months and insisting that the traumatic incident would not alter their plans to do business in Peru.
Employees from a number of big Japanese firms, including Toyota, Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd, NEC Corp and Mitsui Mining and Smelting Co. were among the freed Japanese hostages.

Analysts said the rescue operation would relieve pressure on Fujimori, who had plunged this month in polls due to a growing scandal about alleged human rights abuses by the country's intelligence service.
Now investors would concentrate on the economy's strong fundamentals that has the government aiming for realistic targets of 5 percent growth and single-digit inflation this year, they added.

Fujimori's ruthless fight against Peru's guerrilla groups -- virtually defeating the MRTA and the larger, bloodier Shining Path with the capture of rebel leaders -- saved the economy from the brink of chaos in 1990 with inflation at 7,650 percent.
The president said after the assault that Peru was now at peace, having shown the world it was possible not to give in to terrorism.

But as he lauded Peru's democracy, observers warned the military success of Fujimori's calculated gamble would likley reinforce his autocratic, personalized style and could lead to the weakening of political institutions.

"This enhances his style as a man who does not negotiate. The success should generate enough enthusiasm for Fujimori to be able to change the laws so that he can stand for a third term in 2000," said David Scott-Plamer, a Peruvian guerrilla analyst based in Boston.
